refuted.reason:
Refuted after zooming page-05.png at inset x 960-1610, y 750-1210 and at 4x on the face at x 1180-1340, y 780-920.

(1) Hair. The script explicitly asks for "his hair uncut and loose to the shoulders, bareheaded" in 5.2. It says nothing about curl, and the point of the image is the hair the dungeon later hacked off. The short-hair rule in the Keshavrao lock covers the present-day look, and the present-day Keshavrao in the same panel does have short ragged hair.

(2) Cream tunic and sash. The script calls for "a white angarkha with a sash" and gives no sash colour. The bible's rule against "Nagoji's rust-red turban and sash" (CONTINUITY.md line 132) covers background Maratha riders only. Nothing forbids a red sash on Keshavrao. Nagoji has not yet appeared in a red sash anywhere before this page. I checked Ch1 r6 pages 1-6, including the 6.5 memory: he wears muted rags on a black mare. So no reader can link the sash to Nagoji at this point. The script separates the two memories another way: bay horse (not a black mare), bareheaded (no rust-red turban). The render follows both.

(3) Identity. The face is young, with a faint thin moustache matching the Keshavrao sheet. It is clearly unlike Nagoji's thick curled moustache in 5.1, 5.3 and 5.5. The inset also sits inside Keshavrao's own panel, next to his present-day figure and the "he" caption. It does not read as Nagoji.

(4) Face details. The claimed earlobe stud is the shadow of the ear canal in the middle of the ear, not on the lobe. There is no stud. The forehead dot is about 3 px at 300 DPI (about 0.01 in), invisible in print. It is not forbidden for Keshavrao either: only Nagoji's lock bans forehead marks, and script 3.1 treats forehead marks on Hindu men as fine. The "red lips" belong to a mouth open in song, as the script asks, on a face about 0.2 in wide in print. At print size it reads as a young man singing, not as a woman.

Optional polish only: a saffron or white sash would separate him further from Nagoji's later commander look. The script and bible allow the current art, so this is not a defect.

refuted.description: The Chaul memory inset reads as a young Nagoji, not Keshavrao. The rider has long, loose, curly black hair, a clean upper lip and a broad bright-red sash over a white angarkha. Loose curly hair and a red sash are Nagoji's signature (the commander sheet). The script asks for the same young face as Keshavrao's, and his lock includes a faint moustache. The bible also says memory riders never wear Nagoji's red sash.
refuted.reason:
Refuted. I zoomed into the inset on page 5, panel 5.2 and compared it with the present-day Keshavrao in the same panel and with the approved Keshavrao sheet (07-keshavrao-v15c.png).

1. **The moustache is there.** At 6x zoom the rider has a thin, faint dark moustache on the upper lip, which matches Keshavrao's lock. It looks nothing like Nagoji's thick handlebar moustache. The face is youthful and narrow-jawed with no beard shadow. The dark spot in the ear is the ear canal, not a gold stud, so the "no ear stud" lock also holds.
2. **The long loose hair is scripted.** Script 5.2 asks for "hair uncut and loose to the shoulders". The present-day "hacked short" hair is what the dungeon did to him, so the memory should show it long. Curls are not forbidden. His short hair on the sheet is thick and tousled, which fits curls when grown out.
3. **The script does not specify the sash colour.** It says "a white angarkha with a sash". The bible rule against Nagoji's rust-red turban and sash covers only background Maratha riders in memory and vision panels. It is not a rule for Keshavrao's own memory, and he is not a background rider. The rider also has no turban. Nagoji's commander look is defined by the rust-red turban plus sash.
4. **Other cues point to Keshavrao, not Nagoji.** The horse is a bay, as scripted, not Nagoji's black mare. Nagoji's Chapter 1 memory (ch1 page 6, panel 6.5) shows him with the black mare and no red sash, so readers have no red-sash memory image of Nagoji to confuse this with. The caption "Near Chaul he dared..." sits beside the head-down present-day Keshavrao in the same panel, and the Chapter 2 art never shows Nagoji in commander dress. At print size the rider reads as a younger Keshavrao: slight build, faint moustache, youthful face.

The sash is a bright red that loosely echoes Nagoji's palette. That is at most a matter of taste, since neither the script nor the bible forbids it, and it does not misidentify the character.

refuted.description: The continuity beat planted for Chapter 3 is missing. Keshavrao's right hand should hang at his hip, curled around an absent sword grip. The adaptation notes say Chapter 3 pays this off at his last appearance. Here both his hands are together at his waist, gripping the wrist chain like every other prisoner. He is also seen from the front and side, not from behind as scripted.
refuted.reason: I zoomed in on the fifth figure in page 1, panel 1.5 (page-01.png, around x 910-1110, y 2130-2280 in the original pixels). The art does not show what the reviewer describes. Keshavrao's hands are not together at the centre of his waist. His right hand (on the viewer's left) is a closed fist resting at his right hip, and his elbow is flared out to the side. His left hand sits lower and to the other side, and the slack wrist chain runs between the two hands. The script asks for exactly this at 1.5: the right hand at his hip with fingers curled, the chain slack enough to let it reach there, and the left hand trailing. His pose is also the only one of its kind in the line. The other five prisoners all hold their hands clasped together in front of the belly. So the hilt plant is there and stands out at print size, and it is repeated at 6.2 as the script intends. The one real deviation is the camera angle. The whole line, Keshavrao included, is drawn from the front and side, not from behind, and his head faces forward instead of turning a few degrees toward Nagoji's whisper. That changes the staging, not the beat: his eyes stay forward, and his visible face actually makes the "Keshavrao. One of my riders." caption easier to pin on him. His identity lock also holds (short ragged hair, faint moustache, young face, grey-brown tunic, no ear stud, no scar). At most this is minor polish, not a major missing continuity beat.

refuted.description: The storm beat and its props do not carry through the page. The script builds the storm from props set up in 6.1 (a dipper hanging off true, water slopped in the trough). In 6.5 the frame should be canted clearly more than 6.1, with a spare chain swinging off true and the trough slid against the upright. None of this is drawn: the frame is level and no trough is visible. Instead, rain pours down inside the hold, and a grey open exterior shows at the top right, against the script's 'no exterior, no sky'.
refuted.reason: Refuted. Most of the reviewer's evidence does not match the art. (1) 6.1: the dipper is not hanging straight. At full resolution (top left of the panel) it is tipped off its peg with water spilling from it, and water has slopped over the trough ledges beneath, as the script asks. (2) 6.5 spare chain: there is one. A free chain hangs from the overhead beam ring at about x 740 to 800 of the panel, attached to no one. Its end loop hangs in mid-air above Keshavrao's head, and it is roughly 15 to 20 degrees off vertical. Only the chain to its right runs to Keshavrao's collar. (3) Cant: the heavy post behind Nagoji, which carries his collar ring, leans clearly to the right, about 15 degrees measured on the crop. With the low wide-angle view, this reads as a tilted frame even though the far pillar stays upright. (4) Trough: a long, wet wooden trough-like box sits right against the pen and upright, beside Keshavrao's knee, so 'no trough is visible' is wrong. (5) The grey area overhead is an out-of-focus grating with pale grey light and dark blotchy shapes moving across it. That fits the script's 'grey light at a hatch seam overhead broken by the shadow of running feet', just drawn larger. No sea, sky, horizon or lightning is shown, and the caption box covers much of it. The prayer figure, the canted post, the loose chain and the braced pair are all there, so no beat is missing. The only real remainder is that water streams from the overhead beams onto the wet deck on the right third of the panel. That goes a little past 'only heard and felt'. Still, water through deck gratings in a storm is plausible, and it does not undercut Chapter 3's 'change in the way the ship moved' opening. At most it is a minor polish note (trim the rain to drips at the grating), not a major.

refuted.description: In the Chaul memory inset, Keshavrao can be mistaken for Nagoji. He has long curly hair, a moustache, a cream tunic and a broad red sash, and rides a bay horse, which is Nagoji's commander look (cream tunic, broad red sash) on a horse like Kayal. The standing flag and costume rule reserves Nagoji's red sash and keeps it off Maratha riders in memory panels. The Keshavrao lock says he must never be mistaken for Nagoji.
refuted.reason:
Refuted. The red sash is there: the inset on page 5, panel 5.2 shows a bright red sash over a white angarkha. That alone does not make the rider mistakable for Nagoji, for five reasons.
(1) The face follows the Keshavrao lock, not Nagoji's. In the zoomed crop it is youthful, with a thin, faint moustache and no gold ear stud. Nagoji's identity markers are a thick curled moustache and the ear stud, and both are missing. The long, loose, curly hair is what the script asks for ("hair uncut and loose to the shoulders").
(2) The horse is not Kayal. It is a bay with a white blaze, and CONTINUITY.md says Kayal has "no white markings". Kayal is also not introduced until chapter 7. The script's only horse requirement is "bay horse (not a black mare)", and the art meets it.
(3) By chapter 2 the reader has never seen Nagoji's red sash or cream tunic. His only memory image so far (chapter 1, panel 6.5 in render r6) shows him in drab cloth with a black mare. So nothing on the page invites the comparison.
(4) The rule cited, CONTINUITY.md line 132, is about *background* Maratha riders in memory and vision panels. Keshavrao is the named foreground subject of this inset. The script (5.2) asks for "a white angarkha with a sash" and does not set the sash colour, so a red sash breaks neither the script nor a written lock.
(5) The context makes the identity clear. Present-day Keshavrao sits alone in the same panel, Nagoji is not in 5.2, and the caption "Near Chaul he dared the Portuguese..." points to Keshavrao.
At most, a less saturated sash colour would be optional polish. It is not a costume error of major severity.

refuted.description: The OLD PRISONER's tail does not clearly reach the old prisoner. The balloon "Not this one. The Jesuits need bodies..." sits directly above Nagoji. Its tail runs down alongside Nagoji's hair and stops in open sky beside his shoulder, well above the bowed old prisoner, whose mouth is closed. The line, and the connected "They will work us until we forget our own names", can easily be read as Nagoji's. Extend the tail down to the old prisoner's mouth, or move the balloon over him.
refuted.reason: Refuted. I looked at page 3, panel 3.2 at full resolution. The tail does not stop "well above" the old prisoner. Its tip is at about x496, y1089, and the grey-bearded prisoner's hair starts at about y1096, directly below. That is a gap of about 7 px, roughly 0.6 mm at 300 DPI. At print size the tail touches the crown of his head. The tail also runs past Nagoji instead of ending on him. It passes the left edge of his hair and goes below his chin line before it ends. That is the normal comics way of showing the line belongs to the man behind him, not to Nagoji. Nagoji's mouth is closed and he is looking up, and the old man is the only grey-bearded, older figure in that spot, which matches the OLD PRISONER speaker in the script. Aiming a tail at the speaker's head rather than his mouth is standard practice, so a reader will not credit the line to Nagoji. The linked "They will work us..." balloon follows the same attribution. Nothing here needs a redraw.

refuted.description: The gaol guard is drawn inside the coffle, and the collar-to-collar chain runs across the front of his chest. He reads as a chained man in the line, not a guard walking alongside it. He also stands between the third prisoner and Keshavrao, not at the gap between Keshavrao and Nagoji as the script sets out.
refuted.reason: I'm refuting this as a major problem. I checked page 1, panel 1.5 in crops at full size and at print size. The chain from the grey-bearded third prisoner's collar to Keshavrao's collar does pass in front of the guard's jerkin at upper-chest height. But this is correct overlap, not the guard being chained. His boot sits slightly further up the floor than the prisoners' feet, which puts him further back in the picture than they are. So he is walking on the far side of the chain, which is how "walks alongside the line" looks from this camera angle. He also carries none of the prisoners' irons: no collar (the chain crosses below his neck and doesn't attach), no wrist manacles (his free hand holds a club), and no ankle cuffs (he wears tall boots). He also wears a steel morion and buff jerkin with cross-belts. Even at print size he reads clearly as a guard, not a chained man. The only real point left is his position. He walks between the third prisoner and Keshavrao, one place ahead of where the script puts him. The script line "at the gap between the two men" is ambiguous anyway: it could mean the gap between Nagoji and Keshavrao, or the gap between the two men just ahead of Nagoji. As drawn, he is right next to Keshavrao with his eyes on him, so the danger around the whisper still comes across. Moving him back one place would be a minor polish change, not a major one.

refuted.description: The Keshavrao plant for Chapter 3 is lost. His hands are clasped at the front of his waist like every other prisoner's, with no right hand curled at the hip around an absent grip. His head also turns to screen left, away from Nagoji, not a few degrees toward the whisper. The whole line faces the camera, where the script has Keshavrao and Nagoji seen from behind or in three-quarter back view.
refuted.reason: I zoomed page-01.png at 4x and the art does not support the claim. 1) Hands: Keshavrao's hands are not "clasped at centre front like every other prisoner's". The other five prisoners hold both fists together at mid-waist. Keshavrao's right hand is a separate, tightly curled fist up at the right front of his waist and hip, and his left hand hangs lower near centre, joined only by the slack chain. That roughly matches "right hand at his hip, fingers curled around an absent grip… the left hand trailing with it". It is not a textbook hanging-at-the-side pose, but the difference is small. 2) Head: the line is walking toward screen left, toward the stair. Nagoji, at the back on screen right, faces left in profile, and the whole line leans that way. So when Keshavrao turns his head to screen left, he is looking forward along the line of march, which fits the script's "eyes kept forward". The missing "few degrees toward the whisper" makes no difference to the story. 4.3 says he "has turned his head at last", so not acknowledging Nagoji here fits the arc. 3) Staging: most of the line faces the camera instead of being seen from behind. That is a framing liberty, and it makes Keshavrao (short ragged hair, faint moustache, grey-brown tunic, no ear stud, no scar) easier to identify as the second man ahead of Nagoji. It does not hide the action. 4) Print size: this is a full-width strip with seven figures. Keshavrao's hands are about 0.15 in at print, so no reader would pick out an absent-hilt gesture there either way. The medium shot at 6.2 is the panel that has to carry the Chapter 3 plant, since CHAPTER-03 9.1 is where it pays off. At most this is optional polish on 1.5, not a major defect.

refuted.description: João is not humming. His mouth is shut in a scowl, and he rests a hand on one prisoner's shoulder where the script has him tapping one man, skipping two and cuffing a sleeper. With no pursed lips or head tipped to a beat, the caption 'The same hymn the bells had played.' has nothing in the art to attach to.
refuted.reason: Refuted. The art matches the script's own drawing note for this panel. CHAPTER-02-SCRIPT.md line 236 says "João's humming is drawn as pursed lips; the letterer may add two small musical notes at lettering." I zoomed into João's mouth on page 1, panel 1.2 (crop x400-520, y1040-1130 at full resolution). His lips are closed and pushed forward in a pout, his eyes are half-lidded, and his head is tipped down and to the side. That is a closed-mouth hum drawn as pursed lips, not a scowl. It also differs clearly from his face in 1.3, where he scowls openly with a hard stare and a set mouth. So the caption "The same hymn the bells had played" has something in the art to attach to. The musical notes are optional ("may"), so leaving them out is not an error. On the action: the notched strip is held up in one hand, as the script's first sentence asks. His other hand grips the shoulder of a seated man whose eyes are shut and head is lolled back, which reads as waking a sleeper. The script's "taps one, skips two, cuffs a sleeper" is a sequence that one frozen panel cannot show in full. Shaking the sleeper awake instead of backhanding him is a small change of tone that is hardly visible at print size (the panel is about 2.6 inches wide at 300 DPI). It is not a missing beat. At most it is optional polish: the letterer could add the two musical notes the script allows.

refuted.description: Duarte's gesture reads as a man touching his own chest or cross with downcast eyes. It does not read as a sign of the cross made toward the chain. Nothing links the gesture to the prisoners or to Nagoji, so the planted 'second hesitation' (the blessing that escapes him) is weakened.
refuted.reason: I checked page 2, panel 2.4 at full resolution and zoomed in on the hand (page-02.png, crop around x 1150-1450, y 1480-1780). The art matches the script as written. Script 2.4 says his "ink-stained right hand is raised at his chest, partway through a small, slow sign of the cross". That is what the panel shows. His right hand is the ink-stained one and comes from the screen-left sleeve. The index and middle fingers are extended and held together, which is the standard hand shape for the sign of the cross. They touch his upper sternum, which is the chest stop of the gesture. They sit beside the gold cross, not on it, so he is not fingering the pendant. A reader who knows the gesture will recognize it at print size. The caption in the same panel, "A blessing, perhaps. Or an apology.", settles any doubt. The lowered, tight-jawed look fits the script's "did not plan it" and "something he did not mean to show", and it fits the caption's "apology". The script also calls for the panel to be "tight on Duarte", so the chain was never meant to be in frame. The link to the prisoners comes from the page sequence: in 2.3, Nagoji in his collar faces Duarte directly, and in 2.5 Nagoji watches him leave. The beat has its own panel as the script asks. An outward blessing made in the air toward the chain could read more explicitly, but that is one possible reading of "toward the chain", not a departure from the script's "raised at his chest". It is not a missing beat or a clear error.

refuted.description: João leans back and hauls the chain toward himself, away from the gangplank, while a ship's hand pulls the same chain from the top. It reads as a tug-of-war dragging Nagoji back down the plank, which contradicts both the script ('yanking the chain toward it') and his line 'Faster.'
refuted.reason: I cropped and zoomed panel 3.3, and the tug-of-war reading does not hold up at print size. João stands on the wharf holding the coffle chain with his front arm reaching toward the plank and his rear fist at his belt, a standard handler's grip. His torso is close to upright, not pitched back. His feet are cropped out of the panel, so the reviewer's claim about "weight on his back foot" cannot be checked. The prisoners, Nagoji included, are all shown mid-stride going up the wet plank, and nothing in the art suggests they are being pulled back down. Nagoji's look back over his shoulder is aimed at João, who is speaking, which suits the "Faster" line. The script itself puts João at the foot of the gangplank with the prisoners climbing above him, so any chain he holds has to run up to them, and "yanking the chain toward it" from that position is unclear in the script's own terms. The art's version (a slaver gripping the taut coffle from behind while a ship's hand takes it at the top) is a reasonable reading of that direction, and a reader will see it as the usual driver-with-chain image, not a man dragging Nagoji back down. At most there is a slight ambiguity in how the pull works, which is too small to matter at print size.

minors.description: In the one solo close-up of Nagoji, the face drifts from the V13 sheet. It is broader and fleshier, with soft jowls, a heavy rounded chin and no clear cheekbones, and it reads close to forty. The sheet and the bible specify strong cheekbones, a straight nose and a lean cavalryman's face. The locked traits are all correct (thick curled moustache, clean-shaven chin, small gold stud, long curly hair). The face is still recognisable, but it is the least like Nagoji of any panel in the chapter. A touch-up or regeneration against nagoji-v2.png would bring it in line with 3.2, 4.3 and 6.1.
minors.evidence: page-06.png, close-up at about x 1220-1685, y 830-1250 (original px). Compare with the FRONT and THREE-QUARTER heads on nagoji-v2.png and with the leaner Nagoji faces on page 3.

minors.description: The focal foreground prisoner, back to camera with a chained arm raised against the glare, has long, loose curly black hair like Nagoji's, but he wears an off-white rag. Nagoji is not in this panel's cast, and 2.3 cuts straight to Nagoji over the shoulder. Readers will probably take this central figure for Nagoji and see a costume break, since only Nagoji wears ochre. Either give this figure short or cropped hair so he is clearly an anonymous prisoner, or make him Nagoji in the ochre tunic.
minors.evidence: page-02.png, centre foreground at about x 490-1030, y 970-1250 (original px): long curly hair, off-white wrap over the shoulder, iron cuff on the raised wrist.

minors.description: The gaol guards wear João's costume almost exactly: brown leather vest-jerkins over cream shirts, dark breeches and white stockings. In 1.1 three near-identical small bearded men stand on either side of João on the stair, and the crouching guard in 1.3 is dressed like him too. João reads as the leader of a squad of copies rather than as a distinct character. The script calls for buff (pale yellow-tan) leather jerkins, dented morions or black hats and dark breeches for the guards, which would separate them from João's darker brown jerkin.
minors.evidence: page-01.png, 1.1 top stair at about x 880-1300, y 370-700 (original px), and 1.3 crouching guard at about x 1480-1690, y 1180-1480. The same brown vest, cream shirt and white stockings appear on João on the 11-joao-v15.png sheet.

minors.description: The second instance of the absent-hilt gesture, which Chapter 3 pays off, does not read. The script puts Keshavrao's right hand at his hip, half-curled around a hilt that is not there. Here his right hand is a fist on top of his right knee, which reads as bracing.
minors.evidence: Keshavrao's right forearm is propped on his raised knee with the hand clenched at the kneecap. His left hand lies on his thigh. Nothing is at the hip.

minors.description: The prisoners' costume and irons change between pages 1 and 2. On page 1 the men wear varied grey, brown and off-white sleeveless torn tunics and dhotis, with collars chained collar to collar. In 2.1 every man wears the same long cream tunic tied with a cord. In 2.2 the foreground prisoners show no iron collars, and the chains hang only from their wrists.
minors.evidence: 2.1: five identical cream robe-like tunics. The hands swing apart at each man's sides, farther than a forearm-length wrist chain would allow. 2.2: the foreground men's necks are bare, and a chain hangs from a raised wrist; no collar chain runs along the line.

minors.description: Duarte's props change between two panels of the same moment. In 2.3 he wears a weathered grey-brown felt hat and has a leather satchel strap over his left shoulder. In 2.4 the hat is a crisp black hat with a band, and the satchel strap is gone.
minors.evidence: 2.3: a battered grey-brown hat, and a brown satchel strap from his left shoulder to a bag at his hip. 2.4: a clean black hat with a ribbon band, and no strap on either shoulder.

minors.description: The gate setting is not consistent across the page. 2.2 shows a whitewashed courtyard with a white baroque arched gate. 2.3 shows an iron grille against dark unpainted stone. 2.4 shows golden-stone fortress walls with a round turret and an open wooden gate. 2.5 shows rough grey-gold masonry.
minors.evidence: The courtyard walls in 2.2 are lime-washed white. None of the backgrounds in 2.3 to 2.5 is whitewashed, and the gate is drawn three different ways.

minors.description: The chain setup changes, and the background line has costume confusion. Nagoji's chain in the foreground, and the chains of the men beside him, hang from the collar straight down to the wrist manacles. It is not one chain running collar to collar along the line, as in 1.5, 3.3 and 3.4. In the background line, several men wearing guards' morion helmets carry wrist cuffs like prisoners. The lay clerk wears a brass-hilted sword.
minors.evidence: Foreground: a vertical chain runs from Nagoji's collar ring to his wrist chain, and the old man and the man in the head cloth are chained the same way. Background line: morion-helmeted figures in rag tunics with iron wrist cuffs. The clerk has a sword hanging at his left hip.

minors.description: The chaining and the pen change between two panels scripted as the same two-shot. In 4.3 one slack chain links Nagoji's collar to Keshavrao's and on to a ring on the right post. In 4.4 each collar has its own chain to rings on opposite posts, a new chain runs from each collar down to the wrists, and the two men sit far apart. The lantern also moves from the left post to the background right.
minors.evidence: 4.3: a single chain runs from Nagoji's collar to Keshavrao's collar to the right ring, and a lantern hangs on the left post. 4.4: separate chains go to the left and right posts, vertical chains run from collar to wrists, a wide gap separates the men, and the lantern is behind Keshavrao.

minors.description: Nagoji's bandaging is inconsistent. In 4.2 only two fingertips are wrapped and the back of the hand and wrist are bare. The bible and every other panel show bandaged hands and wrists. From 4.3 to 6.5 his left forearm is wrapped from wrist to elbow, but on pages 1 to 3 both arms have wrist wraps only. This is fine if the change is meant to hide the brand, but it arrives without motivation.
minors.evidence: 4.2: two separate finger wraps; the rest of the hand is bare skin. 4.3, 4.4, 5.1 to 5.5 and 6.1 to 6.5: a long bandage on the left forearm. 1.1, 1.4, 3.2: short wrist bandages only.

minors.description: The setting breaks from the hold on pages 4 and 5. The prisoners seem to sit in an open well, with a wide stretch of sky and the ship's rail above them. The script shows the sky through an open hatch, and 4.5 and 5.4 establish a small hatch and a grating.
minors.evidence: Sky fills about half the frame above the bulwarks, with no hatch coaming or opening framing it. The officer and sailors lean on what reads as the ship's side rail.

minors.description: A background guard wears a long-skirted rust-brown uniform coat and a tricorne-style hat and carries a pike. The script says the gaol guards wear no uniform coat and nothing red, and the other guards on the page wear jerkins and morions. The room behind him, with a tall glazed arched window, also does not match the slit-windowed cellar of 1.1.
minors.evidence: In the left doorway, a figure in a long reddish-brown coat with a cross-belt and a cocked hat stands against a multi-paned arched window.

minors.description: The storm is staged partly outside, against the script lock 'No exterior, no lightning, no sky'. The right third of the panel shows grey open sky with rigging shadows overhead, and rain pours into the hold across the background. This weakens Chapter 3's opening caption, which depends on the storm being felt only from below.
minors.evidence: Page-06, panel 5, upper right (display about x 760-1215, y 1330-1560): an open grey sky with dark rigging silhouettes, and rain streaks falling across the pillars and the praying prisoner.

minors.description: Keshavrao's collar chain climbs taut and nearly vertical from beside his head to a ring on the beam overhead. It reads as a tether from above, the hanging image the script's art constraint forbids ('No chain hangs taut and vertical above a head').
minors.evidence: Page-06, panel 5, about display x 740-800, y 1330-1600: the chain leaves Keshavrao's collar, runs right, then climbs straight up to the beam ring above his head level.

minors.description: The wharf and deck guards wear red capes or tabards and red waist sashes over white shirts. Their morions keep them from reading as British redcoats, but the red breaks the guard costume lock (buff leather jerkin, 'nothing red or blue') used everywhere else in the chapter.
minors.evidence: Page 3, panel 3.2: the morion guard on the ship's platform at about (730, 880) has a red cape or tabard, and the guard at far right at about (1100, 950) has a red shoulder cloth and red sash. Panel 3.4: the guard at left has a red waist sash.

minors.description: The memory inset has a fiery, burning orange edge, not the soft stained edge the script asks for (the same treatment as Chapter 1, panel 6.5). Next to the musket smoke, it can read as an explosion or as the memory burning.
minors.evidence: The inset on the right of panel 5.2 has a flame-coloured scorched border all the way round.

minors.description: The tail for Nagoji's "It is what I know." runs as a long thin line from the far right balloon, along the bottom edge of Keshavrao's "The sahib still counts chances." balloon, to Nagoji's head. It crowds the other balloon and is easy to misread.
minors.evidence: Page-05, panel 3 top strip, display about x 600-800, y 900-945: the tail crosses under Keshavrao's balloon to reach Nagoji.

minors.description: The script marks Nagoji's "Rao." as a whisper, but it is lettered in a standard solid balloon at full size. Use a dashed or whisper balloon, or smaller lettering, so the covert aside reads as one.
minors.evidence: Page 1 render: a standard solid-outline balloon "Rao." at about x1490-1680, y1970-2030, with a tail to Nagoji at the far right.

minors.description: João's hair breaks into the caption box painted into the art. The caption text is pushed to the far right of a wide box, leaving the left 40 percent empty and the box bottom interrupted by his head. Separately, 1.2 is letterboxed shorter than 1.3, so the two panels in row 2 do not share a top edge: 1.3 almost touches 1.1 while 1.2 leaves a wide gap.
minors.evidence: Page 1 render: the caption box is at about x162-905, y972-1055, with the text starting at about x480. João's crown is at about x330-450, y1030-1055. The top of 1.2's border is at about y972, while 1.3's is at about y930.

minors.description: The two caption boxes are cramped. "Father Duarte. I expected triumph," runs to within a few pixels of both the left and right box borders. The boxes butt against the panel border and against each other in a double line with no margin.
minors.evidence: Page 2 render: the caption band is at about x150-910, y1325-1410. In the 2x crop p2_23cap, the text starts about 5 px (at 300 DPI) inside the left border and "triumph," nearly touches the right border.

minors.description: The caption box "A blessing, perhaps. Or an apology." is laid over the left tip of Duarte's hat brim, so the brim disappears under the box.
minors.evidence: Page 2 render: the caption box right edge is at about x1265, y1330-1415, and the brim emerges from under it at about x1270-1300, y1395.

minors.description: In the bottom-right caption, "Someday, I thought, that hesitation might matter.", the text is set flush against the left border of its box with no inner padding. This does not match the other captions on the page.
minors.evidence: Page 2 render: the caption box is at about x928-1680, y2390-2470, and the text starts at about x932.

minors.description: The page layout is uneven. There is a large dead band between the 2.3/2.4 row and 2.5, much larger than the other gutters and the Chapter 1 r6 standard. Also, 2.1 and 2.2 are stacked with widths that differ by only a few pixels on each side, so their edges nearly align but not quite, which looks like an error rather than a design choice.
minors.evidence: Page 2 render: the row 3 bottom is at about y1831 and the 2.5 top at about y1963, a gap of about 130 px (0.44 in), against about 10 px between 2.1 and 2.2. 2.1 spans about x284-1553 and 2.2 about x270-1567.

minors.description: The guard's morion helmet crest pushes up into the caption band and sits directly under the words "land, with". The art collides with the lettering reserve.
minors.evidence: Page 3 render: the caption box is at about x390-1445, y2140-2240. The helmet crest reaches about y2195-2240 at x540-640. Seen in crop p3_34helm.

minors.description: The two caption boxes are oversized, about two thirds of the insert's width and almost its full height. Their text floats in the upper middle of each box, and the boxes cover most of the carved plank this insert exists to show. In "Another prisoner, another ship...", the text also sits flush against the box's left border.
minors.evidence: Page 4 render: the left box is at about x230-620, y880-1130, and the right box at about x1037-1610, y880-1130. The right-box text starts at about x1050. The carved marks are visible only in the strip at about x625-1035.

minors.description: The vertical rhythm is uneven. There are two wide dead bands, between 4.2 and the 4.3/4.4 row and between that row and 4.5, several times the 4.1-to-4.2 gutter. The page feels loosely assembled compared with Chapter 1 r6.
minors.evidence: Page 4 render: the gap between 4.2 (bottom about y1151) and row 3 (top about y1265) is about 114 px. The gap between row 3 (bottom about y1776) and 4.5 (top about y1890) is about 114 px. The gutter between 4.1 and 4.2 is about 10 px.

minors.description: The SAILOR (above) balloon has no black outline, and only a small, unoutlined notch serves as its tail, unlike every other balloon in the chapter. It sits right beside Keshavrao's head, so the off-panel sailor speaker is weakly signalled.
minors.evidence: Page 5 render: a white balloon with no stroke at about x1097-1443, y1605-1745. The tail notch rises to the panel top at about x1135, y1585. Keshavrao's head is at about x1000-1060, y1700. Seen in crop p5_54sailor.

minors.description: The caption box is a flat white rectangle with no black outline, unlike the bordered captions elsewhere. It is far larger than its two lines of text and butts against the panel's top and right borders, covering part of the grey hatch light meant to carry the running-feet shadow.
minors.evidence: Page 6 render: the caption box is at about x1185-1680, y1840-2095, and the text occupies only about y1925-1990.

minors.description: The guard behind Nagoji grips the chain and holds him back, not driving him toward the hatch. Nagoji faces the camera, not looking back once over his shoulder at the town. The script calls for a full-width bottom panel, but it is set about 70 percent wide and centred.
minors.evidence: The panel spans x~385-1455 of 1838 at full res. The guard's gloved fist holds the chain behind Nagoji's back, and Nagoji's face is turned to the viewer.

minors.description: Seen from behind at eye level, not from below. The stone is warm-lit all the way down, with no black-to-white bleach. A church and palms show plainly through the arch at the top. The prisoners wear long cream robes, not the vest-and-dhoti rags of 1.5.
minors.evidence: The crop of x280-1560, y470-780 shows backs climbing a lit stair toward a clear view of a church facade.

minors.description: Duarte's hat changes between consecutive panels: a weathered grey-brown round travel hat in 2.3, then a crisp flat black saturno in 2.4.
minors.evidence: Compare the hat in the 2.3 crop (x150-915, y1320-1830) with the 2.4 crop (x920-1690, y1320-1830).

minors.description: The shipping clerk wears a gold-hilted sword and reads as an officer, not a stout lay clerk. He reads his ledger facing the ship rather than checking it against the prisoner lines. Nagoji dominates the foreground where the script asks for his chain small. The old prisoner's tail passes close to Nagoji's face, which blurs who says 'Not this one.'
minors.evidence: The clerk zoom (x990-1260, y1140-1560) shows a sword at his hip. Nagoji fills the left third of the panel at full height.

minors.description: Nagoji squats with both hands flat against the wall, facing it, so he reads as pushing the wall, not rising slowly off the floor. There is no visible wince, and the script specifies one hand braced.
minors.evidence: The 1.4 crop (x400-1435, y1530-1935) shows both bandaged hands on the wall in a deep squat. The face zoom shows a neutral squint.

minors.description: Two oversized caption boxes cover about 60 percent of the insert, leaving only a narrow strip for the gouged marks and the bandaged fingertips. The text in the right box also sits against its left border.
minors.evidence: The 4.2 crop (x200-1640, y860-1155) shows the boxes filling the left and right thirds and most of the height.

minors.description: Billed as the 'same two-shot' as 4.3, but the two men now sit well apart. Each is chained to a separate ring on opposite posts, and the single slack chain linking both collars in 4.3 is gone. The spacing and chain arrangement change again in 5.1, 5.3 and 6.1.
minors.evidence: In 4.4, Nagoji's collar chain runs to the left post ring and Keshavrao's to the right post ring. In 4.3 one chain runs from Nagoji's collar through Keshavrao's to a single ring at right.

minors.description: The Chaul memory takes half the panel, not a corner inset. It has a flame-like orange edge, not the soft stained edge the script asks for, so it reads as fire. It also shows a Portuguese fort, ships and a church, where the Portuguese should appear only as distant musket smoke.
minors.evidence: The 5.2 crop (x230-1605, y750-1210) shows the right half filled by the vignette with a burning border.

minors.description: Not near dark: the scene is brightly lamp-lit, the frame is not canted, and Keshavrao is not shivering. This removes the baseline that 6.5's steeper tilt is meant to build on.
minors.evidence: A lantern at upper centre-right lights both men warmly. Posts and barrels stand vertical, and the dipper at top left is drawn pouring water.
